corePages.headline: ei, ie und der Reim
corePages.bodyGerman:
ei → [aɪ]  (heißen, mein, zwei)
ie → [iː]   (Sie, wie, wieder)
corePages.bodyEnglish: German vowel pairs trick English speakers: 'ei' sounds like the English word 'eye', 'ie' sounds like 'ee' in see. Mnemonic: when e and i go walking, the LAST one does the talking.
corePages.culturalTip: Say it out loud three times: 'ei = eye, ie = ee'. This one rhyme saves you from misreading half of A1 vocabulary.

corePages.headline: w, v, z und ch
corePages.bodyGerman:
w → [v]   (wohnen, wer, was)
v → [f]   (vier, Vater)
z → [ts]  (zu, zwei, Zoo)
ch → [ç] nach i/e  (ich, nicht)
corePages.bodyEnglish: The letters exist but lie: German 'w' is English 'v', 'v' is English 'f', 'z' is 'ts' as in cats. The 'ch' after i or e is a soft hiss — like saying 'hue' without the vowel.

corePages.headline: Betonnung
corePages.bodyEnglish: German stresses the root of most words: 'WOHnen', 'HEIßen', 'KOMmen'. Loanwords keep English stress: 'KOM-puter', 'HO-tel'. When in doubt, stress the first syllable — even natives will understand you.
corePages.culturalTip: Stress is meaning: 'üBEr' (over) vs 'Über' — okay, that's A2 drama. For now: first syllable.
